claim: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) is a devastating type of injury that results in exacerbated and persistent inflammation followed by fibrosis.
source: The acute traumatic or surgical loss of skeletal muscle, known as volumetric muscle loss (VML), is a devastating type of injury that results in exacerbated and persistent inflammation followed by fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of VML based on established understanding.

claim: Non-healing VML injuries displayed increased pro-inflammatory eicosanoids and a lack of pro-resolving lipid mediators.
source: We observed that non-healing VML injuries displayed increased pro-inflammatory eicosanoids and a lack of pro-resolving lipid mediators.
evidence: This observation is based on metabolipidomics profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of VML with Maresin 1 ameliorated fibrosis through reduction of neutrophils and macrophages.
source: Treatment of VML with a pro-resolving lipid mediator synthesized from docosahexaenoic acid, called Maresin 1, ameliorated fibrosis through reduction of neutrophils and macrophages and enhanced recovery of muscle strength.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including histology, flow cytometry, and functional testing.

claim: Treatment of VML with Maresin 1 enhanced recovery of muscle strength.
source: Treatment of VML with a pro-resolving lipid mediator synthesized from docosahexaenoic acid, called Maresin 1, ameliorated fibrosis through reduction of neutrophils and macrophages and enhanced recovery of muscle strength.
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data showing increased tetanic force.

claim: VML injuries typically result in sustained inflammation, supplantation of muscle tissue with excessive extracellular matrix, and muscle fibrosis.
source: Despite attempts to use regenerative medicine and tissue engineering approaches (Greising et al., 2019), VML injuries typically result in sustained inflammation, supplantation of muscle tissue with excessive extracellular matrix (Garg et al., 2015a), and muscle fibrosis (Greising et al., 2017; Aguilar et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VML results in incessant invasion and accumulation of inflammatory cells such as neutrophils and macrophages.
source: VML results in incessant invasion and accumulation of inflammatory cells such as neutrophils and macrophages that normally protect the wound from infection (Larouche et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: VML drives a dysregulated immune cascade, resulting in increased and prolonged inflammation.
source: However, VML drives a dysregulated immune cascade, resulting in increased and prolonged inflammation (Larouche et al., 2023), inadequate removal of debris, adoption of a fibrotic, TGFβ1-secreting phenotype in macrophages (Chowdary et al., 2023; Larouche et al., 2022), and aberrant regenerative dynamics of tissue-resident stem cells (Larouche et al., 2022; Stepien et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pro-resolving lipid mediators regulate the magnitude and duration of the inflammatory response.
source: Recently, a new class of bioactive signaling factors derived from omega-3 or essential fatty acids called pro-resolving lipid mediators (Serhan, 2014) have been discovered to regulate the magnitude and duration of the inflammatory response (Serhan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pro-resolving lipid mediators restrain the infiltration of neutrophils.
source: These pro-resolving lipid mediators have been shown to restrain the infiltration of neutrophils (Malawista et al., 2008), augment macrophage polarization (Schmid et al., 2016) and phagocytosis (Serhan et al., 2012), and attenuate pro-inflammatory signaling molecules, such as eicosanoids (Serhan and Chiang, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pro-resolving lipid mediators augment macrophage polarization and phagocytosis.
source: These pro-resolving lipid mediators have been shown to restrain the infiltration of neutrophils (Malawista et al., 2008), augment macrophage polarization (Schmid et al., 2016) and phagocytosis (Serhan et al., 2012), and attenuate pro-inflammatory signaling molecules, such as eicosanoids (Serhan and Chiang, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 2-mm punch biopsy defects to murine TA muscles produce fibrotic supplantation and reductions in muscle function.
source: Summing these results shows that 2-mm punch biopsy defects to murine TA muscles (degenerative VML injuries) produce fibrotic supplantation and reductions in muscle function, while 1-mm punch biopsy defects (regenerative VML injuries) result in less fibrosis and functionally recover to the same level as uninjured tissues by 28 dpi.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including histology and functional testing shown in Figure 1.

claim: 1-mm punch biopsy defects result in less fibrosis and functionally recover to the same level as uninjured tissues by 28 dpi.
source: Summing these results shows that 2-mm punch biopsy defects to murine TA muscles (degenerative VML injuries) produce fibrotic supplantation and reductions in muscle function, while 1-mm punch biopsy defects (regenerative VML injuries) result in less fibrosis and functionally recover to the same level as uninjured tissues by 28 dpi.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including histology and functional testing shown in Figure 1.

claim: 2-mm defects showed increased collagen deposition compared to 1-mm defects at 7 dpi.
source: We extracted muscles at 7 and 14 d post injury (dpi) and observed increased collagen deposition in 2-mm defects when compared to 1-mm defects by Picrosirius red staining (Figure 1B–D, n = 3–4 mice per condition, paired).
evidence: This is supported by Picrosirius red staining data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: 2-mm defects showed reductions in force output compared to 1-mm and uninjured muscle at 28 dpi.
source: We found reductions in force output for 2-mm defects when compared to 1-mm and uninjured muscle (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E, n = 6–8 mice per group, unpaired two-way ANOVA), which is consistent with previous studies (Larouche et al., 2022; Anderson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data shown in Figure 1E-F and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: 80 lipid mediators were reliably detected in muscle tissue homogenates.
source: In total, 80 lipid mediators were reliably detected in muscle tissue homogenates (signal-to-noise ratio >3 and peak quality > 0.2 in at least 50% of samples, Supplementary file 1 ).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS/MS metabolipidomics profiling data.

claim: 53 lipid mediators displayed differential dynamics between regenerative vs degenerative VML injuries.
source: Of the 80 analytes detected by LC-MS/MS, 53 displayed differential dynamics between regenerative vs degenerative VML injuries.
evidence: This is based on analysis of LC-MS/MS data.

claim: Degenerative defects showed a greater abundance of many pro-inflammatory eicosanoids including HETEs and prostaglandins.
source: For degenerative defects, a greater abundance of many pro-inflammatory eicosanoids such as the major lipoxygenase-derived hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HETEs) 5-HETE, and 12-HETE, as well as cyclooxygenase (COX)-derived prostaglandins, including PGF2α, PGE2, PGD2, PGA2, PGI2 (6-keto-PGF1α), and TXB2, was detected (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolipidomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PGF2α and 12-HETE remained elevated in concentration for degenerative defects at 7 and 14 dpi.
source: In contrast, PGF2α and 12-HETE remained elevated in concentration for degenerative defects at 7 and 14 dpi (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by metabolipidomics data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: At 14 dpi, degenerative defects showed an overall stronger inflammatory response compared to regenerative defects based on the ratio of eicosanoids to pro-resolving mediators.
source: These data revealed at 14 dpi an overall stronger inflammatory response for degenerative defects when compared to regenerative defects.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the ratio between pro-inflammatory eicosanoids and pro-resolving mediators shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Pro-resolving pathway markers such as 14-HDoHE and 17-HDoHE transiently increased in abundance and returned to uninjured levels by 14 dpi.
source: In contrast to the increased and sustained levels of eicosanoids, pro-resolving pathway markers/biosynthetic intermediates such as from Maresin 1 (14-HDoHE) and D-series resolvins/protectins (17-HDoHE) from clusters 2 and 5 transiently increased in abundance and returned to uninjured levels by 14 dpi (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolipidomics data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Pro-resolving mediators displayed a highly similar trajectory between degenerative or regenerative injuries.
source: The pro-resolving mediators also displayed a highly similar trajectory between degenerative or regenerative injuries (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolipidomics data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in collagen deposition at 7 dpi compared to vehicle-treated controls.
source: At 7 dpi, a significant reduction in collagen deposition was observed by Picrosirius red staining for muscles treated with Maresin 1 compared to vehicle-treated contralateral limbs (Figure 3B and C, n = 9 tissues from nine mice, paired).
evidence: This is supported by Picrosirius red staining data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment resulted in a reduction in macrophage abundance at 7 dpi.
source: Both immunohistochemistry stains for CD68 and flow cytometry quantifications (CD45+F4/80+) revealed a reduction for muscles treated with Maresin 1 compared to vehicle-treated controls (Figure 3D and E), n = 7 tissues from seven mice, paired; (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, n = 8–10 muscles from five mice, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment resulted in significant reductions in neutrophil abundance at 7 dpi.
source: Moreover, consistent with literature showing reduced neutrophil accumulation as a result of Maresin 1 treatment (Francos-Quijorna et al., 2017), flow cytometry at 7 dpi for CD45+Ly6G+ cells revealed significant reductions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, n = 8–10 tissues from five mice, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment resulted in an increase in the cross-sectional area of TdTomato+ myofibers at 7 dpi.
source: We observed an increase in the cross-sectional area (CSA) of TdTomato+ myofibers for tissues treated with Maresin 1 when compared to untreated muscles (Figure 3F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E, n = 4 tissues from four mice, paired).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data from the MuSC lineage-tracing model shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment resulted in a small shift in the distribution of regenerating myofibers with slightly larger MYH3+ myofibers at 7 dpi.
source: In line with our previous observations with the MuSC lineage-tracing model, we detected a small shift in the distribution of regenerating myofibers, with slightly larger MYH3+ myofibers for tissues treated with Maresin 1 when compared to vehicle-treated tissues ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C, n = 11 tissues from 11 mice, unpaired), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Treatment of VML with Maresin 1 yielded increases in maximal tetanic force at 28 dpi compared to vehicle alone.
source: We detected treatment of VML with Maresin 1 yielded increases in maximal tetanic force when compared to vehicle alone (Figure 3H and I, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–E, n = 11 tissues from 11 mice, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by functional testing data shown in Figure 3H-I and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E.

claim: Maresin 1 selectively binds to the leucine-rich repeat containing G-protein-coupled receptor 6 (LGR6).
source: Previous research (Chiang et al., 2019) has demonstrated that Maresin 1 selectively binds to the lleucine-rich repeat containing G-protein-coupled receptor 6 (LGR6), but not other LGR receptors, such as LGR4 or LGR5.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lgr6 expression showed a nearly 65-fold increase among proliferating myoblasts compared to freshly isolated MuSCs and differentiated myotubes.
source: We isolated MuSCs from uninjured hindlimb muscles (Aguilar et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021) and observed low but detectable expression of Lgr6 among freshly isolated MuSCs and differentiated, fused myotubes, with a nearly 65-fold increase in expression among proliferating myoblasts (Figure 4A, n = 3 wells per condition).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment resulted in a significant increase in EdU-positive cells in cultured MuSCs.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we observed a significant increase in EdU-positive cells as a result of Maresin 1 treatment (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, n = 4 wells per condition, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MuSCs treated with Maresin 1 exhibited increased cAMP compared with controls.
source: In line with our previous observations, MuSCs treated with Maresin 1 exhibited increased cAMP compared with controls (Figure 4C, n = 8 biological replicates [three wells per replicate], paired).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment did not change GFP/canonical Wnt signaling in cultured MuSCs from P7Wnt mice.
source: We next isolated MuSCs from uninjured P7Wnt hindlimb muscles, cultured the cells with Maresin 1, and observed no change in GFP/canonical Wnt signaling compared to controls (Figure 4E, n = 6 wells per condition, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by data from the P7Wnt reporter mouse model shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In vivo treatment of degenerative VML injuries with Maresin 1 showed reductions in GFP and canonical Wnt signaling among MuSCs at 7 dpi.
source: In vivo treatment of degenerative VML injuries with Maresin 1 showed reductions in GFP and canonical Wnt signaling among MuSCs at 7 dpi (Figure 4F, n = 3–4 tissues from three mice, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by data from the P7Wnt reporter mouse model shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Slight reductions in active TGFβ1 were observed at 7 dpi in VML-injured muscles treated with Maresin 1 compared to those treated with vehicle.
source: We observed slight reductions in active TGFβ1 at 7 dpi in VML-injured muscles treated with Maresin 1 compared to those treated with vehicle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, n = 3–4 tissues from 3 to 4 mice, unpaired).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 21,679 high-quality scRNA-seq libraries were generated from Maresin 1-treated and vehicle-treated tissues.
source: We generated 21,679 high-quality scRNA-seq libraries from the Maresin 1-treated and vehicle-treated tissues, respectively, encompassing on average 2592 genes per cell with an average read depth of 10,873 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) per cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data processing.

claim: Reductions in neutrophils and dendritic cells were observed in VML-injured tissues treated with Maresin 1.
source: Consistent with immunohistological stains and flow cytometry, we observed reductions in neutrophils and dendritic cells in addition to increases in endothelial cells and MuSCs for VML-injured tissues treated with Maresin 1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Increases in endothelial cells and MuSCs were observed in VML-injured tissues treated with Maresin 1.
source: Consistent with immunohistological stains and flow cytometry, we observed reductions in neutrophils and dendritic cells in addition to increases in endothelial cells and MuSCs for VML-injured tissues treated with Maresin 1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Differential gene expression in macrophages treated with Maresin 1 revealed downregulation of inflammatory signaling genes and genes associated with fibrosis.
source: Differential gene expression in macrophages treated with Maresin 1 revealed downregulation of inflammatory signaling (Ly6c2, Hmox1, Ccl2) and genes associated with fibrosis (Thbs1, Tgfbi, Mmp9), consistent with our histological observations (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Among MuSCs, the predominant gene sets reduced with Maresin 1 treatment were inflammatory, including several transcripts related to interferon signaling response.
source: Among MuSCs, the predominant gene sets reduced with Maresin 1 treatment were inflammatory (Ccl4, Il1b), including several transcripts related to interferon signaling response (Cxcl10, Cxcl9).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Upregulated markers in MuSCs with Maresin 1 treatment included those associated with myogenic differentiation.
source: Upregulated markers in MuSCs included those associated with myogenic differentiation (Mymk, Myog, Ttn) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The lack of pro-resolving mediators and lipid mediator imbalances may contribute to a lack of tissue regeneration after VML.
source: Our data suggest that the lack of pro-resolving mediators and lipid mediator imbalances may contribute to a lack of tissue regeneration after VML.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the metabolipidomics data presented.

claim: Maresin 1 has previously been shown to reduce neutrophil accumulation and alter macrophage phenotype during tissue regeneration.
source: To examine if treatment of degenerative VML with a pro-resolving lipid mediator reduced inflammation and fibrosis, we administered synthetic Maresin 1 (7R,14S-dihydroxydocosa-4Z,8E,10E,12Z,16Z,19Z-hexaenoic acid) (Serhan et al., 2012), which has previously been shown to reduce neutrophil accumulation and alter macrophage phenotype during tissue regeneration (Serhan et al., 2012; Marcon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Administration of Maresin 1 after VML suppresses inflammation and concomitant fibrosis.
source: These results suggest that administration of Maresin 1 after VML suppresses inflammation and concomitant fibrosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Repletion of Maresin 1 positively promotes restoration of function through reduction of inflammation and fibrosis and slight increases in muscle regeneration.
source: These results suggest that repletion of Maresin 1 positively promotes restoration of function through reduction of inflammation and fibrosis and slight increases in muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Engagement of LGR6 in different cell types has been shown to stimulate cyclic AMP and canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Engagement of LGR6 in different cell types has been shown to stimulate several different pathways, including cyclic AMP (cAMP) (Khedgikar et al., 2022) and canonical Wnt signaling (Khedgikar et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2019), which have been associated with MuSC proliferation, migration, and differentiation (Berdeaux and Stewart, 2012; Yin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Maresin 1 stimulates MuSC proliferation via cAMP signaling, and this effect is not mediated through canonical Wnt.
source: Combining these results suggests that Maresin 1 stimulates MuSC proliferation via cAMP signaling, and this effect is not mediated through canonical Wnt, which is consistent with previous results (Khedgikar et al., 2022; Ruan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Sustained Complement activates canonical Wnt signaling and muscle fibrosis.
source: Given sustained Complement activates canonical Wnt signaling and muscle fibrosis (Larouche et al., 2018; Naito et al., 2012), this result was in line with our observations of reductions in collagen deposition and macrophage accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Repletion of Maresin 1 positively impacts MuSCs directly through engagement of LGR6 and indirectly via alterations from myeloid signaling.
source: Our findings indicate that repletion of Maresin 1 positively impacts MuSCs directly through engagement of LGR6 and indirectly via alterations from myeloid signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The regenerative actions of MuSCs are still restrained from fusion due to elevated TGFβ1.
source: However, the regenerative actions of MuSCs are still restrained from fusion due to elevated TGFβ1.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the TGFβ1 ELISA data and previous knowledge.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment may impact other cell types that promote functional recovery such as vasculature.
source: We also speculate that alterations in canonical Wnt signaling in MuSCs from Maresin 1 treatment may be derived through differences in their ability to adhere to the matrix, given that β-catenin interacts with multiple cadherins (Berdeaux and Stewart, 2012; Yin et al., 2013). Additionally, Maresin 1 treatment may impact other cell types that promote functional recovery such as vasculature, which have been shown to precede myogenesis after VML injury (Shcherbina et al., 2020; Jacobsen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: scRNA-seq datasets showed increased recovery of endothelial cells with Maresin 1 treatment.
source: In support of this, our scRNA-seq datasets showed increased recovery of endothelial cells (Chatterjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: Maresin 1 repletion can stimulate MuSC-mediated muscle regeneration after VML and may be promising materials to combine with other regenerative strategies.
source: These observations support that Maresin 1 repletion can stimulate MuSC-mediated muscle regeneration after VML and may be promising materials to combine with other regenerative strategies (Greising et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and suggests future directions.

claim: Open musculoskeletal injuries are responsible for a large fraction of hospital costs and disability payments.
source: In summary, recovery from severe muscle trauma resulting in VML is an unmet clinical need and open musculoskeletal injuries are responsible for a large fraction of hospital costs and disability payments (Garg et al., 2015b; Corona et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The development of strategies to address lipid mediator imbalances may open new paradigms to further explore coupled immuno-regenerative therapies.
source: The development of strategies to address lipid mediator imbalances may open new paradigms to further explore coupled immuno-regenerative (Ho et al., 2017; Palla et al., 2021) therapies.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the findings and previous literature.

claim: Eicosanoids are principal regulators of inflammation.
source: Eicosanoids are principal regulators of inflammation, and we detected increases in pro-inflammatory arachidonic acid-derived eicosanoids such as LTB4, PGE2, and PGF2α as well as other eicosanoid metabolite pathways (5-HETE, 15-HETE) for degenerative VML through all timepoints measured.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and metabolipidomics data.

claim: Neutrophils and inflammatory macrophages produce pro-inflammatory mediators in injured muscle.
source: Given neutrophils and inflammatory macrophages have been demonstrated to produce pro-inflammatory mediators in injured muscle (Giannakis et al., 2019), and we have previously shown persistence of neutrophils in degenerative VML for weeks after injury (Larouche et al., 2022), these results are consistent with increased and sustained inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Short bursts of inflammation and transient exposure to eicosanoids such as COX-derived PGE2 may be beneficial for muscle regeneration.
source: These results suggest that while short bursts of inflammation and transient exposure to eicosanoids such COX-derived PGE2 may be beneficial for muscle regeneration (Ho et al., 2017; Bondesen et al., 2004), longer-term exposure to these signaling factors and concomitant immune dysregulation without balance from pro-resolving lipid mediators (Dort et al., 2019; Markworth et al., 2021b) as observed in degenerative VML are detrimental to muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Longer-term exposure to eicosanoids and concomitant immune dysregulation without balance from pro-resolving lipid mediators are detrimental to muscle regeneration.
source: These results suggest that while short bursts of inflammation and transient exposure to eicosanoids such COX-derived PGE2 may be beneficial for muscle regeneration (Ho et al., 2017; Bondesen et al., 2004), longer-term exposure to these signaling factors and concomitant immune dysregulation without balance from pro-resolving lipid mediators (Dort et al., 2019; Markworth et al., 2021b) as observed in degenerative VML are detrimental to muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: The role of macrophage polarization toward a regenerative phenotype in guiding repair outcomes has been well established and is a critical determinant of development and progression of fibrosis versus successful regeneration.
source: The role of macrophage polarization toward a regenerative phenotype in guiding repair outcomes has been well established and is a critical determinant of development and progression of fibrosis versus successful regeneration (Wang and Zhou, 2022; Wynn and Vannella, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophages do not generate sufficient pro-resolving lipid mediators after VML injury.
source: Our results showing disproportional levels of pro-inflammatory to pro-resolving lipids following degenerative VML injury support that macrophages do not generate sufficient pro-resolving lipid mediators after injury (Giannakis et al., 2019; Halade et al., 2018) and are inhibited from effective transition (Wang et al., 2014; Arnold et al., 2007) toward a regenerative phenotype (Chazaud, 2020; Hymel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Sustained inflammation post degenerative VML injury skews macrophage phenotype toward a fibrosis-promoting subtype.
source: We recently demonstrated that the sustained inflammation post degenerative VML injury skews macrophage phenotype toward a fibrosis-promoting subtype (Spp1+, Trem2+, C1qc+, Cd63+) (Larouche et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Maresin 1 treatment may restore lipid homeostasis and inhibit adoption of a macrophage pathological phenotype.
source: Since fibrosis-promoting macrophages have recently been shown to be regulated by lipid metabolism, these results suggest that Maresin 1 treatment may restore lipid homeostasis and inhibit adoption of a macrophage pathological phenotype (Henderson et al., 2020; Jung et al., 2022; Deczkowska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: LGR6 is expressed on numerous stem and progenitor cells, including in the skin, kidney, and mammary gland, and enhances proliferation, migration, and differentiation.
source: Maresin 1 signaling is mediated in part via engagement of the LGR6 receptor, which is expressed on numerous stem and progenitor cells, including in the skin (Huang et al., 2021), kidney (van Ineveld et al., 2021), and mammary gland (Blaas et al., 2016), and enhances proliferation, migration, and differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lgr6 expression is upregulated in MuSCs after barium chloride injury.
source: This is consistent with previously published bulk RNA-seq datasets isolated from MuSCs after barium chloride injury showing upregulated Lgr6 expression among MuSCs that were isolated after injury (Shcherbina et al., 2020), and suggests that activation of the LGR6 receptor by Maresin 1 may influence proliferation (Khedgikar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of the LGR6 receptor by Maresin 1 may influence MuSC proliferation.
source: This is consistent with previously published bulk RNA-seq datasets isolated from MuSCs after barium chloride injury showing upregulated Lgr6 expression among MuSCs that were isolated after injury (Shcherbina et al., 2020), and suggests that activation of the LGR6 receptor by Maresin 1 may influence proliferation (Khedgikar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: β-catenin interacts with multiple cadherins.
source: We also speculate that alterations in canonical Wnt signaling in MuSCs from Maresin 1 treatment may be derived through differences in their ability to adhere to the matrix, given that β-catenin interacts with multiple cadherins (Berdeaux and Stewart, 2012; Yin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vasculature has been shown to precede myogenesis after VML injury.
source: Additionally, Maresin 1 treatment may impact other cell types that promote functional recovery such as vasculature, which have been shown to precede myogenesis after VML injury (Shcherbina et al., 2020; Jacobsen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The regenerative impact of Maresin 1 treatment is realized principally through both promoting the expansion and differentiation of myoblasts and reducing immune-cell-induced inflammation and fibrosis.
source: Together, these results support the regenerative impact of Maresin 1 treatment being realized principally through both promoting the expansion and differentiation of myoblasts and reducing immune-cell-induced inflammation and fibrosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the scRNA-seq data.

claim: VML defects below a critical size (1 mm) regenerate, while larger VML defects (2 mm) result in long-term increases in fibrosis and reductions in contractile force.
source: Consistent with previous observations in an analogous model in the rectus femoris (Larouche et al., 2022; Anderson et al., 2019), VML defects below a critical size (1 mm) regenerate, while larger VML defects (2 mm) result in long-term increases in fibrosis and reductions in contractile force.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: An imbalance of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids to pro-resolving lipid mediators was detected in degenerative VML injuries.
source: We detected an imbalance of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids to pro-resolving lipid mediators in degenerative VML injuries, which correlates with our previous observations of sustained inflammation and persistent neutrophil (Larouche et al., 2022) and macrophage (Aguilar et al., 2018) presence following degenerative VML.
evidence: This is based on metabolipidomics data and correlates with previous observations.

claim: The imbalance of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids to pro-resolving lipid mediators correlates with sustained inflammation and persistent neutrophil and macrophage presence following degenerative VML.
source: We detected an imbalance of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids to pro-resolving lipid mediators in degenerative VML injuries, which correlates with our previous observations of sustained inflammation and persistent neutrophil (Larouche et al., 2022) and macrophage (Aguilar et al., 2018) presence following degenerative VML.
evidence: This is a correlation based on the current data and previous observations.

claim: Administration of Maresin 1 attenuated fibrosis, reduced neutrophil and macrophage abundance, increased MuSC activation, and partially restored muscle force compared to vehicle-treated controls.
source: Administration of Maresin 1 attenuated fibrosis, reduced neutrophil and macrophage abundance, increased MuSC activation, and partially restored muscle force compared to vehicle-treated controls.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The magnitude and duration of the inflammatory response after muscle injury is a critical determinant of healthy regeneration.
source: The magnitude and duration of the inflammatory response after muscle injury is a critical determinant of healthy regeneration (Tidball, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: After VML, the immune response becomes dysregulated and contributes to fibrotic scarring.
source: After VML, the immune response becomes dysregulated (Larouche et al., 2018) and contributes to fibrotic scarring.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pro-resolving lipid mediators increase in abundance after muscle injuries with barium chloride or cardiotoxin injection.
source: Our observations are distinct from muscle injuries with barium chloride (Schmid et al., 2016) or cardiotoxin injection (Giannakis et al., 2019), where inflammation subsides quickly after injury and pro-resolving lipid mediators increase in abundance.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: Pro-resolving lipid mediators are expressed in VML injuries, but the level at which these factors are detected did not proportionally increase with injury severity and inflammation.
source: While we observed that pro-resolving lipid mediators are expressed in VML injuries, the level at which these factors are detected did not proportionally increase with injury severity and inflammation.
evidence: This is based on metabolipidomics data.

claim: Fibrosis-promoting macrophages have recently been shown to be regulated by lipid metabolism.
source: Since fibrosis-promoting macrophages have recently been shown to be regulated by lipid metabolism, these results suggest that Maresin 1 treatment may restore lipid homeostasis and inhibit adoption of a macrophage pathological phenotype (Henderson et al., 2020; Jung et al., 2022; Deczkowska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TGFβ1 has been shown to attenuate MuSC fusion and becomes dysregulated after VML.
source: We further investigated why stronger enhancements in muscle regeneration were not further enhanced given activation of cAMP and reductions in canonical Wnt by focusing on TGFβ1, which has been shown to attenuate MuSC fusion and becomes dysregulated after VML (Larouche et al., 2022; Girardi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Maresin 1 positively impacts MuSC proliferation through cAMP, but fusion of MuSCs and associated myofiber repair is not significantly enhanced in vivo.
source: Integrating these results supports the notion that Maresin 1 positively impacts MuSC proliferation through cAMP, but fusion of MuSCs and associated myofiber repair is not significantly enhanced in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.
